record.paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
record.original_question: Can genuine discrete layers, motivated by discrete geometry and binary, ternary, or integer-only neural-network representations, be incorporated into neural networks and trained with gradient-descent approaches, or are discrete-optimization approaches better suited to such networks?

evidence.quote: Is it possible to incorporate genuine discrete layers and to train them using gradient-descent approaches? Are there other approaches from discrete optimization better adapted to these networks?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider feed-forward neural networks in which one or more layers are required to be genuinely discrete: the layer's weights, activations, and outputs all take values in a fixed finite or countable discrete set (for example, binary {-1, +1}, ternary {-1, 0, +1}, or integer-valued tensors), and the layer's operation is intrinsically defined on such discrete spaces (motivated, e.g., by discrete geometry or mathematical morphology rather than by quantization of an underlying real-valued layer). Two questions are posed about training such networks end-to-end on a supervised loss:

(1) Is it possible to design genuine discrete layers of this form and incorporate them into a deep network in such a way that the entire network can be trained effectively by gradient-descent–based optimization (possibly via surrogate gradients, relaxations, or other differentiable approximations), achieving accuracy comparable to fully real-valued networks?

(2) Alternatively, are there approaches drawn from discrete optimization (e.g., combinatorial search, integer programming, submodular methods, message passing, or related techniques) that are better suited than gradient descent to training networks composed of such genuinely discrete layers?

Provide a rigorous framework, training algorithm(s), and theoretical or empirical guarantees that resolve which paradigm—continuous gradient-based or discrete combinatorial—is appropriate for training networks with genuine discrete layers.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of how best to train networks with intrinsically discrete layers remains an active and open research direction. Surrogate-gradient and straight-through estimators (e.g., for binary/ternary networks) are widely used heuristics without a definitive theory, and discrete-optimization-based training (mixed-integer programming, combinatorial search) has been explored but not established as superior. No definitive resolution is available.

status_evidence.title: Binary Neural Networks: A Survey
status_evidence.snippet: Training binary neural networks is challenging; surrogate gradients and straight-through estimators are commonly used heuristics.
status_evidence.claim: Training of genuinely discrete (binary) layers is still based on heuristic gradient-surrogate methods, indicating the question remains open.
